lessons.title: Lining up
lessons.objective: You can read a basic formation and count receivers.

payload.prompt: Tap the three receivers in this spread formation.

diagram.alt: A football field showing the offense lined up with three receivers split wide and running backs in the backfield.

explanation.correct: Right. Three receivers split out and one in the slot. That is a passing formation with plenty of options.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the receivers lined up out wide or in the slot. The quarterback and running back are in the backfield.

payload.prompt: What does 11 personnel mean?

options.text: One running back, one tight end, three receivers
Eleven defensive players
One quarterback, one lineman, nine receivers

explanation.correct: Exactly. The first digit is running backs, the second is tight ends. 11 means one of each, leaving three receivers.
explanation.incorrect: Personnel grouping tells you how many running backs and tight ends are on the field. 11 is one back, one tight end, three receivers.

payload.prompt: An empty backfield has no running backs at all, only receivers. True or false?

scene.alt: A football formation with five receivers spread wide and the quarterback alone in the backfield.

explanation.correct: True. Empty means no backs, so five receivers. It signals pass, but it also removes a blocker.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, empty backfield means five receivers and no running backs. It is a passing formation that removes a blocker.

payload.prompt: Tap where the tight end lines up in this I-formation.

diagram.alt: A football field showing the offense in I-formation with quarterback, two running backs in line, and tight end next to the tackle.

explanation.correct: Yes, the tight end lines up on the line of scrimmage next to the tackle. In I-formation, he can block or release as a receiver.
explanation.incorrect: The tight end is the hybrid on the line of scrimmage, usually close to the tackle on either side.

lessons.title: Shotgun and under center
lessons.objective: You can tell shotgun from under center and guess the play type.

payload.prompt: Shotgun means the quarterback is five yards deeper and catches the snap from the center. True or false?

scene.alt: A football formation with the quarterback several yards behind the center, waiting for the snap.

explanation.correct: True. Shotgun gives the quarterback time to see the defense and throw, but removes the handoff option.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, shotgun lines up the quarterback several yards back. It is better for passing plays but harder to run.

payload.prompt: The quarterback is under center on third and short. What is the play likely to be?

options.text: A handoff or a quarterback sneak
A deep pass downfield
A play-action pass

explanation.correct: Right. Under center is better for running and sneaks. Short yardage usually means run the ball.
explanation.incorrect: Under center gives the quarterback an easy handoff. Short yardage usually calls for a run or sneak, not a pass.

payload.prompt: Tap where the quarterback lines up in shotgun.

diagram.alt: A football field showing the line of scrimmage with the center and quarterback positions marked, the quarterback several yards back.

explanation.correct: Right, shotgun lines up the quarterback several yards back, around the 5-yard depth. He catches a snap and throws.
explanation.incorrect: Shotgun positions the quarterback five yards or so behind the center, far enough to see the coverage.

payload.prompt: Match the quarterback positions to their setups.

pairs.definition: The quarterback lines up five yards behind the center and catches the snap in the air.
The quarterback takes the snap directly from the center with the ball handed or snapped into his hands.
The quarterback fakes a handoff or run before looking to throw.

explanation.summary: Shotgun is deep and passing; under center is close and running or faking. Play-action is the hybrid.
explanation.sayThisLine: Shotgun to throw, under center to run, play-action to trick.

payload.prompt: Shotgun is better for running plays because the quarterback has more room to hand the ball. True or false?

scene.alt: A quarterback in shotgun formation attempting to hand the ball to a running back while also showing pass.

explanation.correct: False. Shotgun is actually worse for runs because the quarterback is far back and the handoff is awkward. Under center is better.
explanation.incorrect: No, shotgun makes handoffs harder because the quarterback is so far from the line. Under center is cleaner for runs.

lessons.title: The running game
lessons.objective: You can describe how a handoff turns into yards.

payload.prompt: What does the offensive line do on a run play?

options.text: They block defenders to open a hole for the running back
They try to intercept passes
They line up on the defensive side of the ball

explanation.correct: Exactly. The offensive line's job on runs is to stay in front of their guys and create a gap for the runner to find.
explanation.incorrect: The offensive line blocks. They do not throw or catch. They make holes by moving defenders out of the way.

payload.prompt: Put these steps of a run play in order.

items.text: The center snaps the ball to the quarterback
The offensive line blocks their defenders
items.why: Blockers move first to create gaps.

items.text: The quarterback hands the ball to the running back
items.why: After blockers are moving, the handoff happens.

items.text: The running back finds the hole and runs
items.why: The back accelerates through the open gap.

explanation.correct: Right. The line moves first to create the hole, then the handoff happens, then the back runs through it.
explanation.incorrect: The blocks need to happen before or with the handoff so the hole is open when the runner arrives.

payload.prompt: Tap the open gap the running back should run through.

diagram.alt: A football play diagram showing the offensive line, running back, and defensive players with one clear lane open.

explanation.correct: Yes, that is the hole. The running back plants and accelerates through the opening.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the gap where the blockers have moved their defenders. The runner reads and hits that hole.

payload.prompt: Running backs always follow the play call exactly, even if a better hole opens up. True or false?

scene.alt: A football play with a running back seeing an alternate opening and cutting away from the original play design.

explanation.correct: False. Good running backs read the blocks and cut to the open hole, even if it is not the planned lane.
explanation.incorrect: No, great running backs have vision. They see the blocks develop and take the best gap, not always the design.

payload.prompt: Outside is covered, but a lane opens inside the tackles.

situation.narrative: The play is designed to go outside but the edge is covered and packed with defenders. You see a lane up the middle.

options.label: Cut it back inside where it is open
options.consequence: You find yards and possibly a big play by taking what is there.
considerations: Blockers have opened a hole inside
Live runners take the best gap

options.label: Bounce it to the outside anyway
options.consequence: You run into traffic and get tackled for a loss or minimal gain.
considerations: Forcing a play into a defender loses yards

options.label: Go backward to avoid the defender
options.consequence: Negative yardage and a stalled drive.

payload.expertNote: Vision is the mark of a great back. The play call is a guide, not a law. Read your blockers and find the first crease to daylight. Cutback lanes are often better than the designed edge when the defense over-commits.

lessons.title: The route tree
lessons.objective: You can name the six main routes.

payload.prompt: Match these routes to their descriptions.

pairs.definition: Quick cut across the middle after one to three steps, beating defenders inside.
A straight sprint downfield, the deep shot to take the top off the defense.
Run deep, then cut sharply to the sideline at 8-10 yards to stop the clock.
Run deep, then cut diagonally toward the goal posts for an over-the-middle throw.
Run downfield then sit down in a gap, waiting for the quarterback to throw.

explanation.summary: Five main routes cover all the depths and angles: quick inside (slant), deep (go), sideline (out), middle (post) and settling (curl).
explanation.sayThisLine: Slant in, go deep, out to the sideline, post to the middle, curl to settle.

payload.prompt: Which route breaks the deepest downfield?

image.alt: Three route patterns on a field: a short slant to the middle, a deep post to the middle, and a curl settling in the zone.

options.text: Slant route
options.explanation: Slants break after 1-3 steps, the shallowest route.

options.text: Post route
options.explanation: Post routes go 15+ yards before the break, opening the underneath.

options.text: Curl route
options.explanation: Curls settle around 8-10 yards, medium depth.

explanation.correct: The post route. It runs the deepest before the break, opening up the field underneath.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the route that goes down the field the deepest. The post route goes deep, then cuts toward the middle.
explanation.sayThisLine: Deep routes open up the short stuff underneath.

cues: Post routes go 15 yards or more down the field
Curls settle in a gap at medium depth

payload.prompt: Why do teams throw out routes on the sideline late in a close game?

options.text: Out routes are easier to catch than other routes
The sideline stops the clock when the receiver goes out of bounds
Out routes are always complete passes

explanation.correct: Right. The clock stops when the ball goes out of bounds, which saves time.
explanation.incorrect: Out routes to the sideline stop the clock because an incomplete pass or out-of-bounds is a stopped clock.

payload.prompt: Tap the receiver running the slant route in this play.

diagram.alt: A play diagram showing three receivers: one running slant, one running post, one running out.

explanation.correct: Yes, the slant is the quick route cutting inside. It is ready in 1-2 seconds.
explanation.incorrect: The slant cuts inside quickly. Look for the route heading toward the middle, not deep or wide.

lessons.title: Route lab
lessons.objective: You can build a route so the break comes at the right depth and angle.

payload.prompt: A post route breaks at what depth?

options.text: 3 to 5 yards
8 to 10 yards
15 yards or deeper

explanation.correct: Post routes go deep, usually 15 yards or more before the break. That opens up the underneath.
explanation.incorrect: Posts are deep routes. They go down at least 15 yards before cutting toward the goal posts.

payload.prompt: A curl route always breaks at the same depth every time. True or false?

scene.alt: A receiver running a curl route, settling in the zone at an ideal depth.

explanation.correct: False. The curl is flexible. The receiver sits down in an open zone, which changes based on coverage.
explanation.incorrect: No, curls adjust. The receiver reads where the zone is soft and sits there, not a fixed depth.

payload.prompt: Your out route is tight. Defense is closing on the sideline.

situation.narrative: You are running an out route and the defense is playing tight coverage on the sideline.

options.label: Adjust your break angle up the field
options.consequence: You create separation against tight coverage by reading the defense.
considerations: Good receivers read coverage on the fly
Slight route adjustments beat tight man coverage

options.label: Stick to the sideline cut as designed
options.consequence: The defender is ready for your break and can undercut the pass.
considerations: You lose separation by staying on plan

options.label: Run backward to get away
options.consequence: You abandon the route and the quarterback has no target.

payload.expertNote: Great receivers read coverage on the fly and adjust route breaks slightly to find soft spots. Stick to the fundamental break angle, but let your feet and body angle follow the open space, not the tight defender.

lessons.title: The fake
lessons.objective: You can explain why a fake handoff works.

payload.prompt: Why does a play-action pass work so well?

options.text: Because the defense has to respect the run game, so they move up and open up space behind them
Because the quarterback throws the ball faster than normal
Because the receivers run different routes

explanation.correct: Exactly. If a team has been running the ball well, the defense commits forward to stop the run, leaving the deep field wide open.
explanation.incorrect: Play-action works because it uses the defense's fear of the run against them. They move up, opening the deep middle.

statement.speaker: Announcer
statement.text: That play-action got everybody on the defense. The safety bit on the fake handoff.

payload.question: What just happened?

options.text: The quarterback handed the ball to a running back, who ran for a touchdown
The quarterback pretended to hand the ball, froze the defense, and threw downfield
The defense stopped a run play and the offense had to punt
A defensive player caught an interception

payload.translation: When the safety 'bites' on a fake, he moves up thinking it is a run, leaving the deep middle open for a pass.

followUps.line: Does that only work if the run game is going well?
followUps.why: Tests whether you understand that play-action depends on respecting the running game.

followUps.line: Could they run the same formation and actually hand it off?
followUps.why: Shows you grasp that play-action disguises the real play intention.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, ask: 'Did the quarterback hand the ball or fake it?' The answer tells you everything.

payload.prompt: Play-action works better when the offense has not been running the ball much that game. True or false?

scene.alt: A football play with the defense spread out after play-action, receivers running free.

explanation.correct: False. Play-action works BETTER when the run game is established. The defense respects it more.
explanation.incorrect: No, play-action needs a good run game to work. If the defense does not fear the run, the fake means nothing.

payload.prompt: Tap the linebacker who is out of position after the play-action fake.

diagram.alt: A play diagram showing a play-action with the quarterback faking a handoff while a linebacker crashes forward.

explanation.correct: Yes, the linebacker crashed forward on the fake. Now he is out of position to defend the deep pass.
explanation.incorrect: Look for the defender who moved forward thinking it was a run. Play-action pulls them out of coverage.

lessons.title: Screens and quick passes
lessons.objective: You can say why a screen beats a blitz.

payload.prompt: A screen pass is a short throw to a running back with offensive linemen in front to block. True or false?

scene.alt: A football play showing a screen pass setup with blockers in front of the receiver.

explanation.correct: True. Screens use the rushing defenders' own aggression against them by setting up blockers.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, a screen is a short pass behind the line with blockers set in front. It punishes an aggressive pass rush.

payload.prompt: Heavy blitz is coming and you have a screen pass called.

situation.narrative: The defense is blitzing heavily with extra defenders rushing. You have a screen pass called. What is the advantage?

options.label: Rushing defenders become blockers
options.consequence: The aggressive blitzers are out of position and become your blockers. You gain yards.
considerations: Rushing defenders are away from the ball

options.label: Ball carrier runs deep downfield
options.consequence: Screen passes are short throws. You cannot run deep when designed for the flats.
considerations: Screens are perimeter plays, not deep
Route design does not support depth

options.label: Switch to a field goal attempt
options.consequence: You abandon an effective play call against the blitz.
considerations: Screens are made for blitz situations

payload.expertNote: Screens are the screen pass snare. When a blitz is coming hard, the rushing defenders are out of gaps and perfect for blocking on the perimeter. The aggressive pass rush becomes your advantage.

payload.prompt: When should the offensive linemen move out to block on a screen pass?

options.text: After the ball is caught, they release and get in front
Before the snap, they line up in front
When they see the quarterback throw the screen

explanation.correct: They move after the catch so they are in position as blockers when the back gets the ball.
explanation.incorrect: The linemen stay on the line at the snap, then release downfield after the throw to block.

payload.prompt: Tap where the running back is when the screen pass is thrown.

diagram.alt: A play diagram showing a screen pass with the running back moving into the short passing area.

explanation.correct: In the flats, short and out. The screen hits them right there with blockers setting up.
explanation.incorrect: Screens are short throws. The back is in the flat area near the sideline, not deep.

lessons.title: Tempo and the huddle
lessons.objective: You can spot no-huddle and an audible.

statement.speaker: Announcer
statement.text: They are in a no-huddle offense. The offense lines up quickly without gathering in a huddle.

payload.question: What is the goal of no-huddle?

options.text: The offense saves time and the defense cannot substitute
It is always used on fourth down
The quarterback can skip calling a play
The defense gets to rest more

payload.translation: No-huddle tempo puts pressure on the defense by not letting them substitute fresh players, wearing them down.

followUps.line: Does the offense have to be faster at calling plays in no-huddle?
followUps.why: Tests if you understand the clock pressure on both sides.

followUps.line: Is no-huddle always the best option?
followUps.why: Shows you know teams choose it strategically, not always.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If unsure, think: what does the offense gain by not huddling? Answer: speed and surprise.

payload.prompt: What is an audible?

options.text: When the quarterback changes the play at the line after reading the defense
When the quarterback yells at the defense
A penalty for moving before the snap

explanation.correct: Right. An audible is the quarterback changing the play based on what the defense is showing.
explanation.incorrect: An audible is a pre-snap change. The quarterback sees the defense and switches to a better call.

payload.prompt: A quarterback has 40 seconds on the play clock to call an audible and snap. True or false?

scene.alt: A scoreboard showing the play clock counting down with the quarterback making calls at the line.

explanation.correct: True. The play clock starts at 40 seconds, so the quarterback has that window to signal and execute.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the play clock is 40 seconds. The quarterback must snap by then or it is delay of game.

payload.prompt: Down 3 with 2 minutes left. Huddle or no-huddle?

situation.narrative: It is late in the game, your team is down three points with two minutes left on the clock. You need to score fast to win.

options.label: Go no-huddle and move fast
options.consequence: You maximize plays and save the clock for timeouts. Fast tempo wins tight games.
considerations: Every second counts in two-minute drill

options.label: Use the huddle to discuss plays
options.consequence: Each huddle burns 15-20 seconds. You run out of time with the game on the line.

options.label: Take a knee and punt
options.consequence: Conceding the game without trying. The defense gets the ball back.

payload.expertNote: The two-minute drill is pure tempo. No-huddle offense with sideline throws and timeouts is how you move down the field and get into the end zone under pressure. Every wasted second costs you plays.

payload.prompt: Match these tempo and signaling terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: The offense lines up and gets ready to snap without gathering to discuss the play.
The quarterback changes the play at the line based on seeing the defense alignment.
The 40-second countdown (25 after some stoppages) to snap the ball. Miss it and it is delay of game.

explanation.summary: No-huddle tempo, audible changes, and the play clock pressure all shape how fast an offense moves.
explanation.sayThisLine: No-huddle, audible, play clock: three ways tempo changes the game.
